items.title: Signal Is Building a Way for Admins to Wipe Group Chats From Members’ Phones
items.summary: Signal is preparing to let group admins delete a group’s messages from other people’s phones. The code covers two cases. An admin who removes someone could also wipe the group’s history from that person’s device, and an admin who ends a group could wipe it for every member. Neither is possible today. When an admin ends a group now, Signal’s own Android and Desktop apps tell members they “will still have access to message history”. The changes landed in Signal’s public code between 16 and 19 November 2026, mostly in the iOS app, with small additions to Signal’s server and its shared library. AboutSignal.com , an independent site that follows Signal’s code, spotted them on 25 November. Signal hasn’t announced the feature, and nobody can use it yet. We read the commits ourselves, including a later one that sets the rules for who can trigger a deletion. When we published, we found no coverage beyond AboutSignal and a few forum threads.

items.title: Drupal Warns of New Critical Flaw Exploited in the Wild
items.summary: Drupal fixes a critical flaw exploited in the wild that could let attackers take over vulnerable websites. Drupal has warned of a new highly critical vulnerability in Drupal Core that attackers are actively exploiting to take over vulnerable websites. Tracked as CVE-2026-136716, the flaw is related to improper handling of unusual or incomplete installation states. It is connected to CVE-2026-132165 , also known as Fail2Install, which Drupal patched on November 18. However, the previous fix did not address every vulnerable installation scenario. “ SA-CORE-2026-017 recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer. However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites. It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state.” Drupal maintainers warned . The issue affects websites where the Drupal installer ( install.php ) remains remotely accessible. Drupal stressed that the vulnerability does not affect sites where administrators have already properly secured the installer. One particularly concerning aspect is that administrators cannot easily identify affected installations through the Drupal interface. Moreover, sites that have already been compromised may no longer appear to be in the vulnerable state. Drupal confirmed that CVE-2026-136716 is being exploited in the wild and urged administrators to investigate possible compromises. “ This is being exploited in the wild . Any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised.” continues the advisory. Recommended actions include reviewing logs for unauthorized access and unexpected changes involving the main administrative account, known as user 1 . Administrators should also verify that its email address is under their control and consider resetting its password. The vulnerability has been addressed in the following releases: Drupal 11.4.x: Update to 11.4.14 Drupal 11.3.x: Update to 11.3.23 Drupal 10.6.x: Update to 10.6.23 Drupal 11.0.x through 11.2.x and 10.5.x and earlier are end-of-life and will not receive security fixes. After updating, administrators should run update.php to fix affected installation states and ensure that the installer is properly secured on all existing and new websites. Drupal’s own usage statistics provide further evidence of the exposure. Data published on November 15, 2026, show that thousands of websites still report running Drupal 8.x and tens of thousands use Drupal 9.x, both unsupported branches. Although these figures cover only sites reporting their versions through Drupal’s update system, they highlight the persistence of outdated installations and the need for organizations to migrate to supported releases. This week, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Drupal Core flaw CVE-2026-132165 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog : Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, CMS)

items.title: Occam's Razor in Cyber
items.summary: "Is it a cyberattack?" With all the service failures in recent weeks (from Microsoft 365 to the FAA, Workday and others), this is the number one question my cybersecurity colleagues and I keep hearing. The honest answer is nuanced: sometimes yes, sometimes no, and often it’s something in between.Here is what is easy to miss under the noise: we are in a transition, not a collapse. Frontier AI models applied to code are finding growing numbers of critical vulnerabilities, prompting a rush to patch and update. That may itself contribute to some losses of availability. The preferred destination is infrastructure with less tech debt, fewer exploitable flaws, and higher fault tolerance. Getting there requires discipline, not panic. These five principles can help.PRINCIPLE 1: Trust and reward transparency In the middle of an incident, it can be difficult for organizations to communicate and be clear. However, we must collectively look for and reward clarity, transparency, and communication every time they appear because these traits will make us stronger and better equipped to handle what comes next. In the chaos of an incident, an organization’s culture and preparation will really show (as an aside, check out “Conway’s Law,” which is especially true in a system under stress). Information begins to flow, service returns, and the temptation is to judge and leap to conclusions. I would counsel instead to bring grace, reserve judgment, and offer help as much as possible. And when someone breaks through the chaos, to share information and honest learnings as recognition of that effort. This will build collective resilience.PRINCIPLE 2: Occam’s Razor still applies When competing explanations can account for the same facts, lean into the one that makes the fewest assumptions (often, the simplest explanation). This is Occam’s Razor. Applied to the prevailing question on cyberattacks, the answer, of course, is that it is not always a malicious incident. With nearly 400 failures a week, IT can be unstable at the best of times. However, this is more than a “cluster bias”; that human tendency to try and find meaningful patterns in random data where none actually exist. The number of visible service failures and critical service failures is actually up. We should avoid drawing conclusions without sufficient data. Instead, it’s best to maintain several hypotheses as probable causes and respond as if any of those could be true. For instance, if it could either be a cyberattack or be patch related, take the same approach: act quickly in incident response as if both might be the root cause.PRINCIPLE 3: Turn focus on resilienceAI and workforce reductions will both be convenient scapegoats as organizations face economic pressure. To some extent, either may be a factor. In many cases, neither will be. Reserve judgment. What matters is whether critical services are resilient: whether they have redundancy, failover, and the ability to absorb shocks without cascading. Focus scrutiny there, not on assigning blame before the data is in.PRINCIPLE 4: Operate under the assumption that it might indirectly be security-related For the last 6 months frontier models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s Daybreak have been finding greater numbers of critical vulnerabilities and chains of vulnerabilities that amount to critical severity exposures than ever before. This is leading to a storm of patches and vulnerabilities as more and more companies are applying these models to their code. The result is a rush to patch and update as much as possible as fast as possible, and that is going to lead to some self-inflicted losses of availability. This is actually not only the likely cause of many losses of availability, it is an expected cause of loss of service in the coming weeks. In fact, it is the reason everyone should focus on change management discipline, staged rollouts, and rollback readiness for every patch cycle in the coming weeks.PRINCIPLE 5: Don’t rule out malicious activityHaving said all of this, the root cause can still be cyberattack activity. Frontier-level AI used in offense and toolkits like Artex becoming common in the arsenal of attackers are part of “hacking made easy”. This means that, over time, we have to be following some critical principles in architecture and infrastructure: reducing our attack surfaces, focusing on signal elicitation, deploying deception, building better code (shift left), shielding runtime (shift right), and so on.Bottom Line We have to increase the dialog in a structured way in times of trouble. This means deferring judgment, being transparent, and focusing on availability and supply chain stability in the short term. Strengthen third-party risk management, disaster recovery, and business continuity so that when a supplier goes down, your operations keep running. Architecturally, we know the direction: frontier models and better engineering will produce more functionality with less tech debt, fewer vulnerabilities, and higher fault tolerance. items.title: Multiple Vulnerabilities in Juniper Products Could Allow for Arbitrary Code Execution
items.summary: Multiple vulnerabilities have been discovered in Juniper Session Smart Router and Session Smart Conductor, the most severe of which could allow for arbitrary command execution as root. Session Smart Router is Juniper’s software-based SD-WAN router, and Session Smart Conductor is the management and orchestration platform for a fleet of these routers. Successful exploitation of the most severe of these vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-103406) could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges on the affected Conductor. An attacker with root access could then install programs; view, change, or delete data; or create new accounts with full administrative rights. Because the Conductor manages the router fleet, a compromise could also put every managed site at risk.

items.title: Study Identifies Alarming Volume of Consumer Devices on Healthcare Production Networks
items.summary: A concerning number of consumer devices are being connected to sensitive operational networks, which can provide hackers with a viable pathway into the network and access to sensitive data, according to a recent study by the cybersecurity firm Claroty. The study involved an analysis of more than 45 million devices connected across 30,000+ critical infrastructure locations. The researchers identified a consequential number of consumer devices such as gaming consoles, entertainment devices, and connected cars on production OT, healthcare, and commercial networks. Claroty identified 14,624 gaming consoles connected to healthcare networks. While these devices serve an important purpose in children’s hospitals, they can pose a significant security risk. Gaming consoles and other consumer devices should be isolated from sensitive clinical infrastructure and medical devices; however, the study revealed 13,939 of the healthcare devices (95.3%) were connected to production networks rather than guest or IoT networks. The researchers identified 691 healthcare gaming consoles (4.7%) that were critical or high risk because they contained known vulnerabilities with high CVSS scores, were included in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, had high Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) scores, or had outdated, unsupported, or end-of-life software or firmware. “These devices may appear harmless, but when they share network infrastructure with industrial control systems, building management systems, and medical devices, they can become an entry point for attackers seeking to disrupt production, compromise critical processes, or threaten operational resilience,” explained Claroty. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Medical devices must meet strict cybersecurity standards to be approved by the Food and Drug Administration; however, consumer devices are rarely designed to meet the same security and lifecycle requirements to be connected to operational networks. In many cases, they are not secure by design or default, have insecure communications, and may connect to the internet or cloud services outside the hospital’s control. Further, hospitals are likely to lack visibility into the devices connected to their networks. “The fundamental problem is these devices introduce unmanaged assets, unexpected communications, and potential vulnerabilities into an environment where a compromise can have physical consequences,” warned Claroty. “Despite decades of caution from researchers and security companies, and millions of dollars invested in technology to protect these critical networks, there remain critical failures in virtual network segmentation, continuous threat detection, remote access, and overall governance that still allow for consumer devices to co-exist inside critical operational environments.” Every gaming console connected to a healthcare production network expands the attack surface, creates a security monitoring blind spot, and serves as a potential pivot point for lateral movement. Healthcare organizations can continue to allow these devices to connect to their networks, but they must implement strict network segmentation and only allow them to connect to separate guest or IoT networks with enforced policies. Hospitals should deploy continuous asset discovery to ensure that they have real-time visibility into all devices connected to their networks and enforce policies preventing unauthorized devices from connecting. Without proper governance and network segmentation, these devices could easily provide hackers with an easy entry point into the network.

items.title: New GeoServer RCE exploit chain seen in the wild two days after disclosure
items.summary: Attackers have begun probing a chain of five GeoServer vulnerabilities that enables unauthenticated remote code execution, just two days after the open source geospatial server project disclosed the flaws. Security firm watchTowr, which operates a global network of honeypot servers, reported that it observed the probing activity in the early morning hours of Wednesday. Attackers from multiple IP addresses created stored queries on GeoServer instances, checked whether they were created, and deleted them immediately, a technique that confirms a server is vulnerable without delivering a malicious payload. GeoServer is widely used by government agencies, utilities, and large organizations to publish maps and geospatial data, and it has become a recurring target for attackers. The full RCE chain was reported to the project in August by Jonah Burgess, a senior security researcher at Rapid7 who uses the online handle CryptoCat. The GeoServer project shipped fixes in October and early November but only disclosed the vulnerabilities and published advisories for them on Monday. Chained together, the flaws allow an external unauthenticated attacker to bypass security restrictions, read stored secrets, forge an administrator authentication cookie, and ultimately execute code on the underlying host. They affect GeoServer versions 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.28.0 to 2.28.5, and 2.27.6 and earlier. Users are advised to upgrade to the fixed versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7 depending on which major release they use. A five-flaw chain According to Burgess’ technical write-up this week, one flaw (CVE-2026-129244) uses an overly long stored-query request to trigger a filesystem error that exposes the server’s data-directory path. A second flaw (CVE-2026-129243) allows attackers to call services with a slash in their names, such as x/WFS, bypassing access rules and letting unprivileged users create and delete stored queries, an action normally reserved for administrators. A saved query can then read files from the server, returning the administrator’s password digest along with a cookie-signing key that ships with the default value “geoserver,” a bug tracked as CVE-2026-120705. That key can then be used to forge an administrator cookie (CVE-2026-129245), and a deserialization bug in the database-backed user service finally allows running code with the privileges of the GeoServer process (CVE-2026-129242). Only the final step results in code execution, and only one of the five flaws, the predictable signing key, is rated as critical. Burgess also published a proof-of-concept exploit for the chain. However, researchers from Eye Security independently found a shorter, three-flaw RCE chain that shares the file-read step but reaches code execution through a different bug tracked as CVE-2026-120704 that was also patched. Eye Security used AI models to find the bugs, and the fact that different researchers found some of the same vulnerabilities (two researchers named McCaulay and Quikko are also credited on some of the flaws) highlights the fact that attackers could use AI to find the flaws as well, especially since patches can serve as blueprints for AI agents . In fact, Eye Security had to consider whether delaying disclosure after patches were released was worth the risk of malicious actors finding them independently in the meantime. “We used AI to find these bugs, and a determined attacker with good models could do the same, especially with the official patch to diff against,” Niels Teusink, a security researcher at Eye Security, wrote this week. “That makes the gap between releasing a fix and publishing details riskier than it used to be.” After the advisories were published, it took less than two days for attackers to start probing the flaws to identify vulnerable servers, likely in preparation for attacks. Over 3,000 GeoServer instances are currently exposed to the internet. GeoServer keeps getting targeted This is not the first time GeoServer has been targeted by attackers. In August , a zero-day SQL injection flaw was exploited before a patch was available , and in December 2025 the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) ordered US agencies to patch another GeoServer flaw under active exploitation . Upgrading to a patched release resolves the entire chain, but the patches generate a new cookie-signing key that invalidates existing remember-me sessions. Clustered deployments must set a shared GEOSERVER_REMEMBERME_KEY so nodes sign cookies with the same key, and since the data directory might have been exposed, administrators should also change their passwords. Where patching cannot happen immediately, GeoServer advises blocking requests whose service value contains a slash, removing the remember-me filter from the web filter chain, and checking the data directory’s wfs/query folders for stored queries not created by a legitimate user.

items.title: Linux/EasyShell: MalwareMustDie Identifies One of the Earliest Publicly Documented RATs Built for LoongArch Linux
items.summary: MalwareMustDie analyzes Linux/EasyShell, a Rust implant targeting Linux and macOS, with LoongArch support and stealth features to evade detection. This case began with a shell script found on a victim’s node, which the author credits to 0xrb. MalwareMustDie’s researcher first read it as one more Chinese miner-style uninstaller or downloader. It wasn’t. The script installs software, and what it delivers is a Rust beacon implant. MalwareMustDie wrote four reverse engineering notes, one forensics note, and two OSINT notes, then merged them into one report. That restraint shapes everything that follows. This careful approach guides the entire analysis. The stager is hosted at hxxps://192[.]3.31[.]148:8443 and installs a payload called polkitd on both Linux and macOS. On Linux, it is saved as /usr/bin/polkitd, while on macOS it is placed in ~/Library/Caches/polkitd. The stager randomly chooses one of eight possible file names. The same server hosts the malware and receives its beacon communications over TCP port 8443. It is hosted by ColoCrossing (AS36352) in the United States. The server provides seven different builds: l32, l64, l128, a32, a64, darwin_amd64 and darwin_arm64. The researcher describes the Linux x86 version, l32, as a Rust-based HTTPS beacon with all its required libraries built into the executable. Its build paths contain references to the EasyShell framework, including strings such as easyshell-http-beacon-implant and impl-core. For this reason, the researcher identifies the malware as Linux/EasyShell. The l128 build targets LoongArch, a CPU architecture, and was compiled with rustc 1.96.0, while the others use 1.95.0. According to the researchers, this is one of the earliest publicly documented LoongArch64 RAT implementations he could find in public reporting, identified within the EasyShell multi-platform Rust implant family. “I would like to note that this is one of the earliest publicly documented LoongArch64 RAT implementations I could find in public reporting (as of 2026-11-21), identified within the EasyShell multi-platform Rust implant family. “Earliest” here only means that I found no earlier public analysis; the LoongArch build itself is a framework default ( chapter 7 addendum ).” states the report . “Hands-on access: shell, file theft, credential plugins, SOCKS and relay pivot High. No monetisation code. Operator intent unknown (18.1). The macOS and LoongArch builds are framework defaults offered by every EasyShell stager, not a choice of this operator (18.2).” Two caveats weaken any story about a targeted LoongArch campaign. The report says the macOS and LoongArch payloads aren’t this operator’s choice, because every EasyShell server offers them by default. The author also doubts the LoongArch build would load on a stock Debian loong64 or Kylin host without matching links or a compatible loader, and says it may never have been tested on real hardware. The author didn’t run any sample. The beacon is an HTTPS POST to /api/v2/sync with an X-Client-Id header and a Windows Chrome 131 user agent. According to the report, the implant can open a remote shell, run plugins and scripts, upload and download files, and zip folders. It also offers SOCKS5 and relay tunnels, an outbound proxy, screenshots, process listing and killing, and self-deletion. Credential dumping , token elevation and browser password theft aren’t built in. They come from a separate “Extensions” plugin set. The implant also checks for sandboxes, looking at DMI data, hypervisor names, mouse activity and system resources. Then it renames itself like a kernel thread, for example [kworker/0:0]. A third-party Joe Sandbox run on November 21 gives a useful reality check. It executed another l32 copy on Ubuntu 20.04 for about five minutes. The copy had the same size, 3,769,372 bytes, but a different hash, and it made three TCP connections to the C2, forked a child that called prctl, uname and a thread sleep, and created an empty hidden file. The score was 2 out of 100 with no YARA or Suricata match, which says more about the malware waiting for someone else to show up than about its harmlessness. That hash difference matters. The server writes random bytes into one slot of every payload it generates, so each victim gets a different file. “YARA family rule MMD_Linux_EasyShell_Rust_Implant on memory dumps and new binaries (it still matches the builds without the crate name); do not rely on the hashes for other victims.” MalwareMustDie warns. The first draft of the report dates from November 19, and an addendum on November 22 documented the per-download hashes and the developer repository. On attribution, the author is careful. EasyShell is a Chinese red team C2 framework sold through trial and member programs, and its public repository matches the samples. It isn’t VShell and has no Kinsing or SystemTen link, although the stager is based on a VShell template. No operator is named, and the author says the tool’s build markers describe its build environment, not whoever runs this C2. There’s one loose thread. A separate chapter describes an intrusion on a Chinese mobile-malware hosting server, and a single shell-history line there re-ran the EasyShell stager from the same C2. The author rates the link between the two operators as medium confidence. A note about a December 2025 incident that used the same stager template at a different IP is marked unverified. For security teams, the l32 version does not have its own way to remain on an infected system, although its plugins may add this feature. The researcher suggests looking for processes that use names normally associated with kernel threads, such as [kworker/0:0] or [rcu_sched], but have a real executable file listed under /proc/pid/exe. Another warning sign is HTTPS POST traffic to /api/v2/sync with an X-Client-Id header. On macOS, defenders should look for executable files in user Caches folders that lack a quarantine attribute, code signatures without a Team ID, and security permission requests (TCC prompts) that mention polkitd. The report also includes YARA, Sigma and osquery detection rules. The researcher recommends starting in detection-only mode. These rules were tested against known malware strings, but not against a large collection of legitimate software to check for false positives. If a system looks infected, there is one important rule: do not kill the fake kernel thread immediately. The researcher recommends first isolating and preserving the system before terminating any process. The report ships YARA, Sigma and osquery rules, meant to start in detect-only mode. They were checked on strings, not through a full retro-hunt on legitimate software. “Golden rule: do not kill the fake kernel thread first. Collect its process state and memory, freeze it, cut its network, then clean. Killing it first loses the live config, the session keys and the tunnel table.” concludes the report. items.title: Palo Alto confirms Fragnesia exploitation against firewalls in PHP2Shell attacks
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers exploited Fragnesia, a Linux kernel flaw, to gain root on PAN-OS firewalls through the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, and has shipped fixes six months after the bug was patched in Linux. The vulnerability allows a locally authenticated, low-privileged attacker to escalate privileges to root. “Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” the company said in its November 25 security advisory. It added that all observed attacks targeted devices whose management interface “is exposed to the internet, a configuration our best practices advise against.” Even so, the company labeled the bulletin “Informational” and gave it no CVSS score. Fixed builds span every supported PAN-OS branch from 10.2 to 12.2. A second patch cycle in a month For PAN-OS customers, these are the second set of hotfixes in a month. Between October 25 and October 29, Palo Alto released fixes for PHP2Shell, according to the timeline in its PHP2Shell advisory . PHP2Shell is the collective name for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical flaws in the PHP runtime behind the PAN-OS management web interface. The company rated both flaws 9.2 on CVSS 4.0, and the advisory, which covers PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama, said, “active exploitation has been observed.” The October builds do not include the kernel fix, which arrives in later releases listed in the new bulletin. Even for customers who have patched PHP2Shell, Palo Alto said in the bulletin that it “still recommend[s] upgrading to a fixed release at your next maintenance interval.” Palo Alto is relaxed about the timing. “If you are running a fixed PAN-OS listed in the CVE-2026-109618 advisory, you are protected,” the bulletin said. “The only known way to exploit this vulnerability requires an attacker to first exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerability,” it added. For devices with management access restricted to trusted internal IP addresses, it advises upgrading “at your next maintenance interval.” Duncan Brown, group vice president and global domain lead for worldwide security and trust at IDC, said that the approach is defensible when vulnerabilities are chained. “It’s acceptable to apply one patch that effectively breaks the chain. Ideally, all vulnerabilities would be patched as early as possible, but in many cases this is not practical,” Brown said. Rahul Karne, a senior digital forensics and incident response analyst, called patching PHP2Shell a reasonable short-term step, but said it blocks the known way in without fixing the bug. “The key word is ‘known,’” Karne said. He pointed out that public exploit code for Fragnesia, including a Metasploit module, is available, and that any other code execution flaw on the device would make the kernel bug usable again. From web shell to root The chain has been public for almost a month. In late October, Dream Security researchers reported that attackers combined PHP2Shell with Fragnesia to compromise firewalls running vulnerable PAN-OS builds. According to Dream, the attackers used PHP2Shell to run code as the web service account and then used the kernel flaw to become root. From there, they tunneled into internal networks and stole credentials, private keys, and network topology data. The kernel bug itself is not new. William Bowling, a researcher at Zellic, disclosed Fragnesia on May 13 along with a proof-of-concept exploit and an upstream kernel patch, after finding it with the help of the company’s V12 AI auditing agent. Fedora shipped a fixed kernel the next day. Karne said some delay is normal for appliance vendors that maintain custom kernels across many hardware models, but 195 days is too long when exploit code is public. Customers should hear whether they are affected within a week of such a disclosure and get a fix within about 30 days, he said. “A firewall should not get security fixes more slowly than the servers it protects,” Karne said. The firewall as a foothold Palo Alto is not the only security vendor whose appliances were rooted this way. In November, Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers were hit after attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Gaia OS privilege escalation flaw to take over gateways and deploy a wiper. Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said CISOs should treat the incident as a weakness in their trust model for security appliances, not merely a patching issue. “A firewall running Linux, PHP and other third-party components must be assessed with the same rigor as any privileged, internet-facing server,” Daftary said. “Vendor labels such as ‘Informational’ should never override enterprise risk analysis when flaws can be chained to achieve root access.” “If a device is exposed during the attack window, merely applying the hotfix does not establish trust,” she added. Teams should review administrative access, rotate credentials and certificates, hunt for persistence, and reimage the appliance from a known-good build when root compromise cannot be ruled out, she said. Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers exploited Fragnesia, a Linux kernel flaw, to gain root on PAN-OS firewalls through the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, and has shipped fixes six months after the bug was patched in Linux.

The vulnerability allows a locally authenticated, low-privileged attacker to escalate privileges to root.

“Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” the company said in its November 25 security advisory. It added that all observed attacks targeted devices whose management interface “is exposed to the internet, a configuration our best practices advise against.”

Even so, the company labeled the bulletin “Informational” and gave it no CVSS score. Fixed builds span every supported PAN-OS branch from 10.2 to 12.2.

A second patch cycle in a month

For PAN-OS customers, these are the second set of hotfixes in a month. Between October 25 and October 29, Palo Alto released fixes for PHP2Shell, according to the timeline in its PHP2Shell advisory. PHP2Shell is the collective name for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical flaws in the PHP runtime behind the PAN-OS management web interface.

The company rated both flaws 9.2 on CVSS 4.0, and the advisory, which covers PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama, said, “active exploitation has been observed.”

The October builds do not include the kernel fix, which arrives in later releases listed in the new bulletin. Even for customers who have patched PHP2Shell, Palo Alto said in the bulletin that it “still recommend[s] upgrading to a fixed release at your next maintenance interval.”

Palo Alto is relaxed about the timing. “If you are running a fixed PAN-OS listed in the CVE-2026-109618 advisory, you are protected,” the bulletin said. “The only known way to exploit this vulnerability requires an attacker to first exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerability,” it added. For devices with management access restricted to trusted internal IP addresses, it advises upgrading “at your next maintenance interval.”

Duncan Brown, group vice president and global domain lead for worldwide security and trust at IDC, said that the approach is defensible when vulnerabilities are chained.

“It’s acceptable to apply one patch that effectively breaks the chain. Ideally, all vulnerabilities would be patched as early as possible, but in many cases this is not practical,” Brown said.

Rahul Karne, a senior digital forensics and incident response analyst, called patching PHP2Shell a reasonable short-term step, but said it blocks the known way in without fixing the bug.

“The key word is ‘known,’” Karne said. He pointed out that public exploit code for Fragnesia, including a Metasploit module, is available, and that any other code execution flaw on the device would make the kernel bug usable again.

From web shell to root

The chain has been public for almost a month. In late October, Dream Security researchers reported that attackers combined PHP2Shell with Fragnesia to compromise firewalls running vulnerable PAN-OS builds.

According to Dream, the attackers used PHP2Shell to run code as the web service account and then used the kernel flaw to become root. From there, they tunneled into internal networks and stole credentials, private keys, and network topology data.

The kernel bug itself is not new. William Bowling, a researcher at Zellic, disclosed Fragnesia on May 13 along with a proof-of-concept exploit and an upstream kernel patch, after finding it with the help of the company’s V12 AI auditing agent. Fedora shipped a fixed kernel the next day.

Karne said some delay is normal for appliance vendors that maintain custom kernels across many hardware models, but 195 days is too long when exploit code is public. Customers should hear whether they are affected within a week of such a disclosure and get a fix within about 30 days, he said.

“A firewall should not get security fixes more slowly than the servers it protects,” Karne said.

The firewall as a foothold

Palo Alto is not the only security vendor whose appliances were rooted this way. In November, Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers were hit after attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Gaia OS privilege escalation flaw to take over gateways and deploy a wiper.

Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said CISOs should treat the incident as a weakness in their trust model for security appliances, not merely a patching issue.

“A firewall running Linux, PHP and other third-party components must be assessed with the same rigor as any privileged, internet-facing server,” Daftary said. “Vendor labels such as ‘Informational’ should never override enterprise risk analysis when flaws can be chained to achieve root access.”

“If a device is exposed during the attack window, merely applying the hotfix does not establish trust,” she added. Teams should review administrative access, rotate credentials and certificates, hunt for persistence, and reimage the appliance from a known-good build when root compromise cannot be ruled out, she said. items.title: Australia’s Flight Centre Data Breach Exposes Customer Records and Passport Details
items.summary: Australia’s Flight Centre is investigating a third-party breach that exposed customer travel records and limited passport details. Australia’s Flight Centre Travel Group is investigating a cyber incident involving a third-party accommodation booking system that may have exposed a significant number of customer records. The company disclosed the incident on November 26, saying it had detected unusual activity in a platform used by several of its leisure travel brands. The breach affects the accommodation system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout and some independent agents. Flight bookings and corporate travel bookings, which rely on separate systems, haven’t been affected. According to Reuters, the company has not yet determined how many records were taken. Its initial investigation found that most of the accessed records contained customer names, while some also included basic travel details. “Flight ⁠Centre said some of its leisure travel brands — the Flight ​Centre brand, Travel Associates and Cruiseabout — and some independent agents ​used the third-party accommodation booking system. The company said the unusual activity did not affect flight bookings.” Reuters states . “The company said it had not yet ​determined how many records the activity extracted, but its initial ​review showed most accessed records contained only customer names, while some also ‌included ⁠basic travel information” The exposed data may include more sensitive information. Flight Centre believes a very small number of records contained passport details, email addresses, phone numbers and dates of birth. In rare cases, records may also have included health or mobility information, which can be particularly sensitive when linked to travel plans. So far, the company has found no evidence that credit card, payment or bank account details were accessed. However, the exposed personal and travel information could still be used for targeted scams, identity theft and social engineering attacks. The incident highlights a common problem with third-party suppliers. A booking platform may store customer information collected by several brands and independent travel agents. This means that a single attack on a shared system could expose data belonging to several businesses at once. Flight Centre has activated its incident response plan and is investigating the incident with the supplier and cybersecurity firm Mandiant. The company says it is working to identify affected systems, contain the incident, improve security, change authentication keys and passwords, and increase monitoring. It is also notifying the relevant authorities and working with external security experts. The investigation is still ongoing, and the company has not confirmed how many customers were affected or when the suspicious activity started. Flight Centre says existing hotel bookings can go ahead as planned and that it will contact customers whose data may have been exposed. For customers, the main concern is how attackers could use the stolen information. An email mentioning a real hotel, booking reference or travel date can look genuine, especially when it arrives shortly before a trip. Flight Centre has advised customers to be careful with unexpected emails, phone calls or messages about their bookings. They should avoid clicking links, opening attachments or sharing personal information, passwords or payment details in response to unsolicited requests. The warning is worth taking seriously even if no payment data was exposed. Travel details provide context that criminals can use to make phishing attempts more credible, and a request to “confirm” a booking or passport detail may be the next step in an attack. Flight Centre said it would contact affected customers and apologised for the concern the incident may cause. “Flight Centre is warning customers to be cautious of “unexpected emails, calls or messages” about their bookings, and to “not click on links, open attachments or share personal information, passwords or payment details in response”. ABC News states . “The company apologised to affected customers, noting “that an incident like this can be unsettling”.” Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, Flight Centre)

items.title: Cardiology Associates of Mobile and Teklinks Pay $1.25M to Settle Data Breach Lawsuit
items.summary: Cardiology Associates of Mobile and its IT service provider, Teklinks, Inc., have agreed to pay $1,250,000 to settle a class action lawsuit stemming from an October 2024 data breach. Cardiology Associates of Mobile is an Alabama-based provider of cardiovascular care serving patients in Alabama and Mississippi. Teklinks is an Alabama-based provider of IT, managed services, and cloud solutions. The security incident was identified on October 22, 2024. Hackers were determined to have breached the network of Cardiology Associates of Mobile and gained access to the names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, health insurance information, and medical information of 172,678 current and former patients. Multiple class action lawsuits were filed in response to the data breach. The lawsuits had overlapping claims and classes and were consolidated into a single complaint – In re Cardiology Associates Data Breach Litigation – which is pending in the Circuit Court for Mobile County, Alabama. The plaintiffs allege that the defendants were at fault for failing to implement adequate cybersecurity measures to protect sensitive data. The consolidated class action lawsuit asserted claims for negligence, negligence per se , and breach of implied contract. Cardiology Associates of Mobile and Teklinks disagree with all claims and contentions in the litigation, including claims of wrongdoing and liability, while the plaintiffs believe their claims have merit. A separate lawsuit was filed by Cardiology Associates of Mobile against its IT vendor asserting claims for breach of contract, indemnity, and declaratory relief. The lawsuit was dismissed with prejudice in May 2026 in connection with the settlement agreement. All parties agreed to explore the possibility of an early resolution to the litigation, and following mediation, the terms of a settlement were agreed upon by all parties. Under the terms of the settlement, the defendants have agreed to pay $1,250,000 to pay benefits to the class members, after attorneys’ fees and expenses, settlement administration costs, and service awards for the nine class representatives have been deducted. Class members may claim a 24-month membership to a credit monitoring service. In addition, a claim may be submitted for reimbursement of documented, unreimbursed losses due to the data breach up to a maximum of $4,000 per class member. A claim may also be submitted for a pro rata cash payment. The cash payments will exhaust the settlement fund. The deadline for opting out and filing an objection is November 30, 2026. The deadline for submitting a claim is December 29, 2026. The final fairness hearing has been scheduled for January 29, 2027. items.title: Spyware Victims in Four EU Countries Face Eight Barriers to Justice, CDT Europe Report Finds
items.summary: If a government hacks your phone in the EU, you will probably never be told. A new report says that’s only the first of eight barriers victims run into. The Centre for Democracy & Technology Europe, the Brussels office of the US digital rights group CDT, published Navigating the Labyrinth on 26 November. Written by Sarah Graham and Rand Hammoud, it looks at Greece, Hungary, Poland and Spain, where people hacked with spyware they believe their own state used are trying to get redress in court. It draws on court files, published research and interviews held in summer and autumn 2026 with victims, their lawyers and advocates. The report doesn’t say how many people were interviewed, and it names them only where they agreed. It covers commercial spyware bought by states, such as Pegasus and Predator, not tools governments build themselves. When we published, the report had been shared on Bluesky by CDT Europe and a few people who work on spyware. We found no news coverage of it.

items.summary: U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds HPE, Danfoss, Mitel MiCollab, and Vates Xen Orchestra flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the following HPE, Danfoss, Mitel MiCollab, and Vates Xen Orchestra flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog . CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability The first flaw, tracked as CVE-2023-25914 (CVSS score of 7.5), is a path traversal vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration management systems running software versions prior to 3.3. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit improper restrictions on file paths to retrieve and read files from the underlying system through the XML interface. Access to sensitive files could provide information useful for further compromising the device. There are no publicly confirmed reports of exploitation in the wild or threat actors associated with this vulnerability. Danfoss addressed the issue in software version 3.3. The second flaw, tracked as CVE-2023-25915 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical improper input validation vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 800A systems running software versions prior to 3.3. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient input validation to execute arbitrary commands on the target system, potentially gaining full control of the affected refrigeration controller. Despite its critical severity and the potential consequences for operational technology environments, there are no publicly confirmed reports linking this specific vulnerability to attacks in the wild or identifying threat actors exploiting it. Danfoss released software version 3.3 to address the issue. The third flaw, tracked as CVE-2025-41450 (CVSS score of 8.2), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series systems running software versions prior to 4.2. The authentication bypass allows an attacker to generate web reports without proper authorization, potentially exposing sensitive information such as internal IP addresses, usernames and store names. The vulnerability was identified by researchers at Claroty’s Team82. Although it affects the same family of refrigeration controllers targeted in the European supermarket attacks, there is no public confirmation that attackers exploited this particular CVE during those incidents. Danfoss addressed the vulnerability in software version 4.2. The fourth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-103406 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical OS command injection vulnerability affecting HPE Juniper Session Smart Conductor. The flaw resides in the AutomatedProvisioner component and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges by supplying a specially crafted Salt minion ID. The vulnerability has been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, confirming exploitation in the wild. However, no specific threat actor or ransomware campaign has been publicly attributed to these attacks. Administrators should apply the security updates provided by Juniper, including versions 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3 for the affected release branches. The fifth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133275 (CVSS score of 5.3), is an unrestricted file upload vulnerability affecting the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of Mitel MiCollab. The vulnerability affects MiCollab version 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient file type validation to upload arbitrary files to the target system. Depending on the nature of the uploaded files and the system configuration, this could provide an opportunity for further malicious activity. Mitel has not reported confirmed exploitation in the wild or identified any threat actors associated with this vulnerability. The company released a security patch for affected installations. The sixth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133303 (CVSS score of 9.0), is a critical XML injection vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient parameter validation and leverage malicious content staged in advance to perform XML injection and execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system. Successful exploitation could compromise the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the affected installation. Mitel has not disclosed any confirmed exploitation in the wild or identified threat actors behind attacks exploiting this flaw. A security patch is available for affected MiCollab installations. The seventh flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133311 (CVSS score of 5.9), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker who knows a specific system-generated random identifier or has access to malicious content staged in advance could exploit the weakness to obtain sensitive information. The vulnerability is limited to the affected functionality and does not provide unrestricted access to arbitrary files elsewhere on the system. No confirmed exploitation or associated threat actors have been publicly reported. Mitel has released a security patch to address the issue. The eighth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133323 (CVSS score of 10.0), is a critical OS command injection vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient parameter sanitization to perform blind command injection and execute arbitrary commands within the context of the affected system. Successful exploitation could compromise system integrity and availability. Mitel has not reported confirmed exploitation in the wild or attributed attacks to specific threat actors. A security patch is available to address the vulnerability. The ninth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133324 (CVSS score of 5.3), is an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. Improper handling of authentication could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass security controls and perform unauthorized actions within the application. Successful exploitation could compromise the security of the affected installation. No publicly confirmed exploitation or associated threat actors have been reported. Mitel has released a security patch for the affected versions. The tenth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133469 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical authentication bypass vulnerability affecting Vates Xen Orchestra, a management and backup platform for XCP-ng and XenServer environments. The vulnerability affects versions prior to 6.9.2 and 6.10.1. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit improper handling of authentication tokens by supplying a specially crafted cookie containing an empty JSON object. The application may then authenticate the attacker as the owner of an existing, unexpired token. Once authenticated, the attacker could retrieve reusable authentication token identifiers, potentially enabling persistent unauthorized access to the environment. The vulnerability is actively exploited in the wild , although no specific threat actors have been publicly identified. Vates addressed the issue in Xen Orchestra versions 6.9.2 and 6.10.1. The Danfoss vulnerabilities deserve particular attention because they affect the same family of refrigeration management systems involved in the cyberattacks targeting European supermarkets in October and November 2026. The first wave of attacks, detected between October 11 and 12, compromised refrigeration controllers at approximately 700 retail sites in France. Attackers manipulated defrost settings, forcing refrigeration equipment to operate at excessively high temperatures. The incidents resulted in substantial food losses and at least 15 reported fires. A second wave between November 1 and 2 affected retailers across several other European countries. The French authorities’ investigation attributed the October attacks to Shahid Kaveh , a cyber unit associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). However, responsibility for the subsequent November attacks across Europe has not been conclusively established. The technical evidence points to the exploitation of internet-exposed refrigeration management interfaces, with default credentials and outdated firmware considered likely entry points. However, investigators have not confirmed that CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915 or CVE-2025-41450 were specifically exploited during these operations. The incidents instead highlight the risks associated with exposing operational technology (OT) systems directly to the internet without adequate authentication, network segmentation and security updates. An additional development is worth mentioning: a November 2026 advisory from Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre reported research by Midnight Blue identifying six previously unknown pre-authentication remote code execution vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM 800A controllers, affecting firmware versions up to and including 5.3.2. At the time of the advisory, these flaws had not yet received CVE identifiers and no patches were available. Researchers also warned that attackers could establish persistence surviving factory resets and firmware updates. These findings add another layer of concern to the security of refrigeration infrastructure. ncsc.gov.ie According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities , FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog. Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure. CISA order U.S. federal civilian agencies to remediate eight of them by November 28, 2026, and the remaining two by December 9, 2026. The individual deadlines are: November 28, 2026: CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915, CVE-2026-103406, CVE-2026-133275, CVE-2026-133303, CVE-2026-133323, CVE-2026-133324 and CVE-2026-133469. December 9, 2026: CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2026-133311. Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA )

Once authenticated, the attacker could retrieve reusable authentication token identifiers, potentially enabling persistent unauthorized access to the environment. The vulnerability is actively exploited in the wild, although no specific threat actors have been publicly identified. Vates addressed the issue in Xen Orchestra versions 6.9.2 and 6.10.1.

The Danfoss vulnerabilities deserve particular attention because they affect the same family of refrigeration management systems involved in the cyberattacks targeting European supermarkets in October and November 2026.

The first wave of attacks, detected between October 11 and 12, compromised refrigeration controllers at approximately 700 retail sites in France. Attackers manipulated defrost settings, forcing refrigeration equipment to operate at excessively high temperatures. The incidents resulted in substantial food losses and at least 15 reported fires. A second wave between November 1 and 2 affected retailers across several other European countries.

The French authorities’ investigation attributed the October attacks to Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). However, responsibility for the subsequent November attacks across Europe has not been conclusively established.

The technical evidence points to the exploitation of internet-exposed refrigeration management interfaces, with default credentials and outdated firmware considered likely entry points. However, investigators have not confirmed that CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915 or CVE-2025-41450 were specifically exploited during these operations. The incidents instead highlight the risks associated with exposing operational technology (OT) systems directly to the internet without adequate authentication, network segmentation and security updates.

An additional development is worth mentioning: a November 2026 advisory from Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre reported research by Midnight Blue identifying six previously unknown pre-authentication remote code execution vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM 800A controllers, affecting firmware versions up to and including 5.3.2. At the time of the advisory, these flaws had not yet received CVE identifiers and no patches were available. Researchers also warned that attackers could establish persistence surviving factory resets and firmware updates. These findings add another layer of concern to the security of refrigeration infrastructure. ncsc.gov.ie

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA order U.S. federal civilian agencies to remediate eight of them by November 28, 2026, and the remaining two by December 9, 2026. The individual deadlines are:

  • November 28, 2026: CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915, CVE-2026-103406, CVE-2026-133275, CVE-2026-133303, CVE-2026-133323, CVE-2026-133324 and CVE-2026-133469.
  • December 9, 2026: CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2026-133311.

items.title: What is Strategic Threat Intelligence? | Recorded Future
items.summary: Key Takeaways Threat intelligence is often thought of as a single function, but in reality, it can be broken down into four categories: strategic, tactical, operational, and technical. Strategic threat intelligence is non-technical and is used by high-level strategists to inform specific decisions. For the most part, strategic threat intelligence comes from freely available sources. However, the volume of available sources, combined with language constraints, often makes manual collection infeasible. The success of strategic threat intelligence depends on strong two-way communication between threat analysts and their primary audience — usually the board of directors. On the surface, threat intelligence appears to be a single discipline, closely intertwined with the cyber threat intelligence cycle . Practitioners collect data from a variety of sources, analyze it, and use the outputs to make decisions. The reality is a little more complicated. As with most specialties, threat intelligence can be broken down into subcategories, each with its own uses, techniques, and challenges. Here are the three distinct categories that threat intelligence is typically boiled down to: Strategic Intelligence : Non-technical, risk-based intelligence used by high-level decision makers. Tactical Intelligence : Details of threat actor tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). Operational Intelligence : Actionable information about specific incoming attacks. In this blog series, we’ll take an in-depth look at each of these categories, including how they are collected, analyzed, and used to enhance security. Today, we’re covering strategic intelligence. What Is Strategic Threat Intelligence? Strategic threat intelligence is non-technical, risk-focused intelligence that provides executives and board members with a bird’s-eye view of an organization’s threat landscape, enabling them to understand the broader impact of high-level business decisions. It isn’t concerned with specific actors, indicators, or attacks. Given that the audience is primarily C-suite and board level, strategic threat intelligence is almost exclusively non-technical. Instead, it covers factors such as risk scores and the possible outcomes of a given action or decision, such as entering a foreign market or taking an ideological position. Since it’s used to inform specific, high-level decisions, strategic threat intelligence is usually gathered on demand rather than as an ongoing initiative, and is most often presented as a report or briefing. Sources of Strategic Threat Intelligence Unlike other intelligence categories, the majority of strategic threat intelligence sources are Open Source Intelligence, or OSINT , meaning they can be freely accessed by anyone who cares to do so. Common examples include: Policy documents from nation-states and other groups of interest Local and national media Industry- and subject-specific publications Comments, online activity, and articles from individuals of interest Free content produced by security organizations (e.g., white papers, research reports, etc.) While the accessibility of strategic sources can be a tremendous positive, it can also be a double-edged sword, as analysts must manually process huge quantities of raw data in order to identify valuable insights. Worse still, the most valuable insights are often “hidden” in foreign language sources, forcing analysts to spend even more time on translation. Fortunately, if analysts are armed with the right tools, these difficulties can largely be sidestepped. Powerful threat intelligence solutions can scour a large volume of sources, identify relevant information in real time, and automatically translate non-native results. Who Produces Strategic Threat Intelligence? Perhaps the most significant difference between strategic threat intelligence and other intelligence categories is the skill set needed for production. While typical security and analysis skills are still essential, producing strategic threat intelligence also requires a great deal of expertise in other areas — in particular, a strong understanding of sociopolitical and business concepts. Since this broad skill set is rarely found in a single individual, some organizations hire analysts with state or military intelligence backgrounds and train them in the security-specific subject areas required for the role. While this approach takes time and resources to pull off, it is often quicker and more effective than holding out for the perfect applicant. How Should Organizations Request Strategic Threat Intelligence? Strategic threat intelligence stands apart from the other three categories because it’s almost exclusively requested by (and produced for) a non-technical audience. While the outputs are produced in a format that senior executives and board members will understand, the audience’s lack of understanding of what is and isn’t possible can lead them to make requests that non-government analysts simply can’t meet. For example, if an organization’s board were considering expansion into another country, it might call on its threat intelligence analysts to provide some insights. As we’ve already seen, though, strategic threat intelligence is very much a “made-to-order” discipline, meaning analysts will do their best to meet the specific requirements of their board. This is where “asking good questions” comes in. An inexperienced (in the context of threat intelligence) board might be tempted to demand, “Tell us how, where, and by whom we’ll be attacked if we open this branch.” Requirements like this are highly unlikely to lead to valuable insights for two reasons: Acquiring detailed intelligence on specific local or national actors is often impossible for non-state actors. Attempting to predict specific attacks is far less useful (and reliable) than understanding the most common threat trends and their relative likelihoods. A far better line of questioning would be, “Is this expansion likely to open us up to increased cyber risk? If it is, which threat vectors are most likely to be employed, and what would be the cost of preparing for or responding to those threats?” This type of question gives analysts far greater scope to explore useful avenues of research and is much more likely to result in an insightful and actionable intelligence product. Ideally, there should be an open line of communication between an organization’s board and its threat intelligence specialists — most likely via the CISO — to ensure that strategic threat intelligence project parameters are set in a way that’s conducive to producing an actionable output. How Is Strategic Threat Intelligence Success Evaluated? As we’ve already seen, strategic threat intelligence outputs rarely include binary “yes or no” recommendations, focusing instead on variables such as risk and confidence scores. But that’s not to say that evaluation can’t (or shouldn’t) be attempted. A strong feedback loop is essential to the consistent production of high-quality intelligence products. Just like any intelligence initiative, a strategic threat intelligence capability should be subject to ongoing evaluation. This evaluation process should include feedback from the intelligence team’s primary audience — typically the board of directors — and answer key questions, such as: Was the intelligence produced in line with requirements? How helpful was the intelligence in making the stated decision? Was the intelligence pitched correctly for its (likely non-technical) audience? This type of feedback will typically be collected informally by the CISO and should be used to improve future strategic intelligence gathering and presentation. Of course, one obvious question remains: Was the intelligence proven accurate over time? Unfortunately, this question often proves extremely hard, if not impossible, to answer, for two primary reasons: Strategic intelligence deals primarily with measurements of risk and likelihood, so even if an anticipated result doesn’t occur, that doesn’t mean the intelligence was inaccurate. It’s rarely possible to determine precisely what has (or hasn’t) happened in a remote situation. With all that said, the accuracy of strategic intelligence should be monitored as far as possible and used to improve processes and intelligence outputs. What’s the Difference Between Strategic and Tactical Threat Intelligence? As we’ve already seen, threat intelligence breaks down into three primary categories — strategic, tactical, and operational — and it’s easy to conflate strategic with tactical since both inform security decisions. The difference comes down to who’s using the intelligence and what they do with it. Strategic Threat Intelligence Tactical Threat Intelligence Audience Executives, boards, and other high-level decision-makers Security analysts, SOC teams, and incident responders Focus Broad risk trends and business impact Specific threat actor tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) Data Sources Open-source policy documents, media, and industry research Malware samples, attack patterns, and technical indicators of compromise Output Format Reports and briefings for non-technical stakeholders Technical indicators that feed directly into security tools Primary Use Informing decisions like market expansion or risk tolerance Detecting and defending against specific, active threats In short : strategic intelligence tells leadership whether and why a risk matters to the business, while tactical intelligence tells defenders how an attack works so they can stop it. For a closer look at how tactical intelligence is gathered and applied, see our breakdown of tactical threat intelligence . Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between strategic and operational threat intelligence for government agencies? Strategic intelligence informs long-term policy and risk decisions for government leadership, while operational intelligence supports response to specific, imminent threats or incidents — the same distinction that applies in the private sector, though government strategic intelligence often incorporates geopolitical and nation-state sourcing more heavily. What are some real-world examples of strategic threat intelligence? Examples include geopolitical risk assessments before entering a new market, industry-wide threat landscape reports for board presentations, and executive briefings on how a competitor’s breach might signal shared industry risk. What are the benefits of using strategic threat intelligence for business decisions? It gives leadership a clearer, evidence-based view of risk before making high-stakes calls — like market expansion, M&A, or vendor selection — reducing the chance of decisions made on incomplete or purely anecdotal information. How long does it typically take to produce a strategic threat intelligence report? Timelines vary by scope, but since most strategic intelligence is made-to-order rather than continuously monitored, turnaround often ranges from a few days for a narrow question to several weeks for a comprehensive board-level briefing. Today, we’re covering strategic intelligence.

What Is Strategic Threat Intelligence?

Strategic threat intelligence is non-technical, risk-focused intelligence that provides executives and board members with a bird’s-eye view of an organization’s threat landscape, enabling them to understand the broader impact of high-level business decisions. It isn’t concerned with specific actors, indicators, or attacks.

Given that the audience is primarily C-suite and board level, strategic threat intelligence is almost exclusively non-technical. Instead, it covers factors such as risk scores and the possible outcomes of a given action or decision, such as entering a foreign market or taking an ideological position.

Since it’s used to inform specific, high-level decisions, strategic threat intelligence is usually gathered on demand rather than as an ongoing initiative, and is most often presented as a report or briefing.

Sources of Strategic Threat Intelligence

Unlike other intelligence categories, the majority of strategic threat intelligence sources are Open Source Intelligence, or OSINT, meaning they can be freely accessed by anyone who cares to do so. Common examples include:

  • Policy documents from nation-states and other groups of interest
  • Local and national media
  • Industry- and subject-specific publications
  • Comments, online activity, and articles from individuals of interest
  • Free content produced by security organizations (e.g., white papers, research reports, etc.)

While the accessibility of strategic sources can be a tremendous positive, it can also be a double-edged sword, as analysts must manually process huge quantities of raw data in order to identify valuable insights. Worse still, the most valuable insights are often “hidden” in foreign language sources, forcing analysts to spend even more time on translation.

Who Produces Strategic Threat Intelligence?

Perhaps the most significant difference between strategic threat intelligence and other intelligence categories is the skill set needed for production. While typical security and analysis skills are still essential, producing strategic threat intelligence also requires a great deal of expertise in other areas — in particular, a strong understanding of sociopolitical and business concepts.

Since this broad skill set is rarely found in a single individual, some organizations hire analysts with state or military intelligence backgrounds and train them in the security-specific subject areas required for the role. While this approach takes time and resources to pull off, it is often quicker and more effective than holding out for the perfect applicant.

How Should Organizations Request Strategic Threat Intelligence?

Strategic threat intelligence stands apart from the other three categories because it’s almost exclusively requested by (and produced for) a non-technical audience. While the outputs are produced in a format that senior executives and board members will understand, the audience’s lack of understanding of what is and isn’t possible can lead them to make requests that non-government analysts simply can’t meet.

For example, if an organization’s board were considering expansion into another country, it might call on its threat intelligence analysts to provide some insights. As we’ve already seen, though, strategic threat intelligence is very much a “made-to-order” discipline, meaning analysts will do their best to meet the specific requirements of their board.

This is where “asking good questions” comes in. An inexperienced (in the context of threat intelligence) board might be tempted to demand, “Tell us how, where, and by whom we’ll be attacked if we open this branch.”

Requirements like this are highly unlikely to lead to valuable insights for two reasons:

  • Acquiring detailed intelligence on specific local or national actors is often impossible for non-state actors.
  • Attempting to predict specific attacks is far less useful (and reliable) than understanding the most common threat trends and their relative likelihoods.

A far better line of questioning would be, “Is this expansion likely to open us up to increased cyber risk? If it is, which threat vectors are most likely to be employed, and what would be the cost of preparing for or responding to those threats?” This type of question gives analysts far greater scope to explore useful avenues of research and is much more likely to result in an insightful and actionable intelligence product.

Ideally, there should be an open line of communication between an organization’s board and its threat intelligence specialists — most likely via the CISO — to ensure that strategic threat intelligence project parameters are set in a way that’s conducive to producing an actionable output.

How Is Strategic Threat Intelligence Success Evaluated?

As we’ve already seen, strategic threat intelligence outputs rarely include binary “yes or no” recommendations, focusing instead on variables such as risk and confidence scores. But that’s not to say that evaluation can’t (or shouldn’t) be attempted.

A strong feedback loop is essential to the consistent production of high-quality intelligence products. Just like any intelligence initiative, a strategic threat intelligence capability should be subject to ongoing evaluation.

This evaluation process should include feedback from the intelligence team’s primary audience — typically the board of directors — and answer key questions, such as:

  • Was the intelligence produced in line with requirements?
  • How helpful was the intelligence in making the stated decision?
  • Was the intelligence pitched correctly for its (likely non-technical) audience?

This type of feedback will typically be collected informally by the CISO and should be used to improve future strategic intelligence gathering and presentation. Of course, one obvious question remains: Was the intelligence proven accurate over time? Unfortunately, this question often proves extremely hard, if not impossible, to answer, for two primary reasons:

  • Strategic intelligence deals primarily with measurements of risk and likelihood, so even if an anticipated result doesn’t occur, that doesn’t mean the intelligence was inaccurate.
  • It’s rarely possible to determine precisely what has (or hasn’t) happened in a remote situation.

With all that said, the accuracy of strategic intelligence should be monitored as far as possible and used to improve processes and intelligence outputs.
